argument: Baudrillard argues that Western society was already living in a postmodern condition by the early 1980s, in which signs and media images have detached entirely from reality, becoming 'copies of copies' that people mistake for the real thing. In this fragmented, media-saturated world, people build identity through consumption of signs whose meanings are set by the media, and events like the Gulf War are experienced by most people only as a simulation of images and sound bites rather than as the reality of the conflict itself.
keyIdeas: Post-structuralists claim categories like sane versus insane aren't written into the universe: all we ever have access to are cultural and scientific constructions attempting to describe reality, not capital-T Truth.
Unlike other early-1980s thinkers who thought postmodern effects were decades away, Baudrillard argued Western society was already living in a postmodern condition.
The Matrix is only a loose illustration, not a literal claim: Baudrillard means that a network of signs can obscure people's ability to see reality, not that we live in a literal computer simulation.

With grand narratives fragmented, mass consumerism becomes one common way (not a logical necessity) for people in advanced-capitalist societies to express identity by buying 'signs' whose meanings are set by the media, images that have become 'a copy of a copy of a copy' disconnected from anything real.

Baudrillard's claim that the Gulf War 'did not take place' means that for most people, all they ever accessed was a narrow stream of media images and sound bites, not the actual reality of the conflict.

terms.def: An imitation of a real-world process or system that becomes disconnected from what it originally depicted.
A word or image, like a purchased product, that stands in for a concept such as personality or status.
A totalizing, unifying story (religious, political) that people historically used to build identity around.

terms.term: copy of a copy of a copy
terms.def: The process by which signs, having once imitated reality, are repeatedly reimitated by media and life until disconnected from anything real.
The postmodern condition of no longer having grand narratives available to build a stable identity around.
